summary.name: Performance, Scalability, and High Availability: 3 Key Infrastructure Adaptability Requirements
summary.one_liner: A guest post on High Scalability by Tony Branson that distinguishes performance, scalability, and high availability in infrastructure and argues for database load balancing and failover as a way to achieve them.
use_cases: Explaining the difference between performance, scalability, and high availability
Planning database failover for a middle-tier application
Deciding between horizontal and vertical scaling
Evaluating whether to buy more servers or optimize first
Designing database load balancing for business continuity
summary.what_it_does: The article defines performance as throughput under a given workload, scalability as handling growing workload or demand, and high availability as applications staying accessible when servers fail. It lists failover requirements such as identical components on every node, failover aware of node availability and location, and task tracking with rollback. It warns against over-optimization and buying excess infrastructure, suggesting scaling plans based on service level agreements. It presents database load balancing software, which sits between applications and database servers, as the way to reroute traffic on failure and scale without application changes.
notable: Clear definitions separating performance, scalability, and high availability
Argues against over-optimizing and buying more infrastructure than needed
Describes database load balancing as transparent to applications
caveats: Written as a guest post with a vendor-leaning tone; the load balancing product is not named
Cost figures ($30,000 server, $100,000 scalability effort) are illustrative examples from the author, not verified data
